utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Ball.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman will now continue. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And good morning, Dr. Ball. How are you this morning? Did you get some rest last night? Feel better?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Felt well last night. How did you rest?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not as well, probably.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll bet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I spent a lot of time last night and early this morning considering what I might ask you about today, and I have significantly restructured my questions in the hope that they are simple and can be answered in many cases with just a yes or no answer. I think we might be able to finish fairly quickly if you can cooperate in trying to answer yes or no if possible. I have no objection to your giving explanations when you think them necessary, however. Okay. In the Milosevic trial at page 2178, you -- you told the Chamber that 45 per cent of the material that you considered regarding KLA activity was provided to you by the OTP and that 55 per cent of it came from open sources. Can you tell this Chamber what were these open sources that you got the 55 per cent of this information from.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this at some length yesterday, I believe. It was in appendix 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. It's nothing beyond what's in appendix 3?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you engage in any kind of reliability checking regarding material received from those open sources?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we did with the death reports, we checked all of the sources against each other so that the same events would not be counted in multiple ways. Many sources report the same events and we strove to count each event only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that would be more of an integrity check than a reliability check, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how you're using those two terms. Perhaps you could define them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. When I say an integrity check, to check that you're not doubling up data. When I say reliability check, I'm talking about a check on whether or not the data you were being provided is true?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm not an investigator. I did not go to Kosovo and investigate the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As to the OTP information, you were asked in the same part of the Milosevic transcript if that was provided to you in the form of statements or in statistical or summarised form, and your answer to that question by Mr. Nice was: "It was provided in highly summarised form." Now, what do you mean when you character the information as being "highly summarised"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given a spreadsheet. The spreadsheet contained fields which described the very brief summary of the event in text as well as date and place information. There were several other fields that were redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So like the material that came from open sources, with this material from the OTP, you also had an opportunity to independently verify the validity of that information?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm not an investigator. I did not go to Kosovo and investigate cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday at page 89, line 21, in answer to similar questioning you said that the ICTY provided you with a database of materials. Is that this spreadsheet that you're talking about or was there an additional database of materials that was provided to you by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the KLA activity, this is the only material that was provided to me. There were also a number of other sources that were also provided to me on other topics. We've discussed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You do know at the time that the OTP provided you with this information regarding KLA activity that the OTP had certain theories about this case, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the indictments, if that's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. And engaging your assistance, what they were looking for was help from you in supporting those theories as contained in the indictment, as you appropriately mentioned.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way that Mr. Nice or any of his colleagues characterised what they were looking for from me. They said they wanted me to provide a statistical evaluation of the patterns of these four phenomena.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I suspect you'll agree they wouldn't have found you very useful if your analysis had destroyed their theories?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently, my opinion of Mr. Nice is somewhat higher than yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one second. What are the four phenomena?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: KLA and Serb police interactions, so KLA activity is the first of the phenomena; NATO air-strikes is the fourth -- second of the phenomena, excuse me; killings of Kosovar Albanians is the third; and migration of Kosovar Albanians, the fourth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Distinguishing between migration and killing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 9624 yesterday you said this in how you weigh certain evidence: "Evidence that goes against the interest is much more weighty than evidence that goes in favour of interest." Now, if that's your approach, since a great deal of your data came from the OTP, did you consider that it might have less weight than other data?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk now about your hypotheses and they're listed in the report; there are three of them. The first one is action by the KLA motivated Kosovars to leave their homes, either directly because the KLA ordered people to leave, or indirectly because Kosovars fled fighting between KLA and Yugoslav forces. Now, to analyse and deal with this hypothesis, you needed to have the most reliable and complete information about KLA activity that you could get your hands on; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I could get my hands on, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And you got no information directly from the KLA, did you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the only information that you had was information that came either from the OTP or from these other open sources that you have referred to.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, principally, the information came from Yugoslav sources -- both in the ICTY data and in my own research.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did the OTP ever give you a statement or a copy of testimony of the Chief of the General Staff of the KLA, Mr. Bislim Zyrapi?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was -- I never received any testimonies whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told this Chamber yesterday that 60 per cent of the peaks in killing and migration occur with no prior NATO or KLA activity. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was derived from a table and we can consider it. I can't confirm the statistic without referring to the table, but you can continue with your question while we look it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wouldn't it have been fair to say that no prior NATO or KLA activity that we know about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. If there was independent KLA activity or NATO activity that you didn't know about that coincided with killing or migration, that could have a profound effect on your results, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not a profound effect. It would have to be systematic and overwhelming for it to have a profound effect. Finding one or two municipalities or even three or four municipalities in which that was the case would have relatively little effect. Again, as we discussed yesterday, the peaks and valleys method is a weak method for evaluating the causality between these patterns. You and I discussed this at some length yesterday and you indicated that you had difficulty finding the points in my research where I made the reservations about that. I've since revised the research and I can point you to several other places where we make precise this reservation --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse, sir, if I may finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm happy with where we got yesterday with that. I really don't want to go into that anymore, unless the Judges want to hear from you about it then you can of course talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is you want to say, Dr. Ball?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yesterday Mr. Ackerman brought this up at some length and now he seems to be bringing it up again notwithstanding his demurral and he complained yesterday that he was unable to find our reservations. I pointed him to one of those reservations and I would like to point out another of those reservations in case he is not able to find this one as well. It is on the second page of our 19 February 2002 report in the discussion section, and it says: "The primary drawback of this method is that it considers only the effect of the hypothesised cause on the hypothesised effect at the time of the effect's peak or maximum point." We go on to discuss a subtler and finely ingrained analysis and refer to the regression analysis as far more appropriate for a causal analysis. Therefore, to get back to your earlier question, where you implied that somehow finding additional KLA or NATO activity would have a profound effect on our findings, I cannot agree. As we said in each of these papers and our reservations about this technique, the technique is not sufficiently finely grained to make a clear determination about rejecting causes. So perhaps that helps clarify my disagreement with your earlier statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You just told us a moment ago that if the -- if you had found conflicting data for as many as three or four municipalities it probably wouldn't have changed your conclusion. How many municipalities did you actually analyse?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them, 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So four would be like one-sixth of 29, and if your data was incorrect regarding one-sixth of those 29, isn't that a fairly profound number, a high percentage?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is actually precisely why I asked the Bench's leave to review the 19 February report and my conclusions I just read. Mr. Ackerman is drawing unreasonable conclusions about the efficacy of this method. Even if all 29 municipalities coincided with one specific peak, with the peak in that municipality, if there were NATO and KLA activity coinciding with that peak, that would be an inadequate basis for finding that NATO or KLA activity were the cause of that activity. The reason is explained in, I believe, fairly clear language in section 1.2 of the 19 February 2002 report, which you have, in which we discuss - and I used this metaphor yesterday - that coincidence does not imply causation. Now, I understand that you're very adept at logical streams, so I assume you understand that one or should we review it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, don't review it.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is, Mr. Ackerman, you're giggling notwithstanding, that you cannot find that simply because the sun rises and later that day there are killings or refugee flow, that the sun's rising has caused them. The coincidence of killing and migration is an inadequate basis on which to make the conclusion that the NATO or KLA activity may have caused it; rather, we need to see not only the coincidence but the common absence of the two, so that if there is killing or migration without NATO or KLA activity we must ask what has motivated that. If we look at the graphs, we see that many times there are coincidences whereby there has been some killing or migration on the same day as bombing or KLA activity but in many more instances there is killing and migration without such activity. So focusing, I believe, on this point with your proportions merely distracts the Court from the broader point which we have made repeatedly throughout these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Going back to what you said a moment ago about even if all 29 municipalities coincided with one specific peak, if there were NATO and KLA activity coinciding with that, would that not undermine your conclusion that NATO and KLA activity was inconsistent with the movement of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- that's a good question and I think that to answer it we might want to consider a particular graph and ask ourselves about a specific pattern. So if we could look at the graph for Djakovica on page 10 of my January 2007 report, we'll get a bit more detail on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we notice that there is a single KLA action and a bombing that coincide with the peak of killing and precede a peak of migration very early in the period late March/early April, but then there is a series, and that is the kind of coincidence that we're talking about here. However, then there's a series of KLA activities and NATO air-strikes that are not -- that do not correspond -- oh, I'm sorry, this is not the correct -- the graph that's shown on the screen is not correct. I'm not sure if you would like me to pause. This is -- I'm looking at the Decani graph from the 2007 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you were looking at Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Djakovica, yes. Decani is on the same page. It's page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we have it in hard copy so you can carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So there's a series of bombing and KLA activities that follow those peaks, and what's striking is that the bombing and KLA activity that follow the peaks are not -- do not coincide with any peaks. A causal argument would suggest that continuing bombing or continuing KLA activity would cause continuing killing or continuing migration if the killing -- excuse me, if the bombing and KLA activity were causes. So the question that Mr. Ackerman has raised is what if all 29 or some high fraction of the 29 municipalities had the pattern we see for Djakovica, where there is, in fact, a coincidence. My response is it's not just the coincidence of the peaks that matters. We need to see both the coincidence when there's a positive effect and the coincidence when there's a negative effect. What we get here is the coincidence when there's a positive effect we get killing and migration rising after a KLA action and a bombing, but then a series of KLA and NATO actions that are not followed by any significant killing or migration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, with, you know, huge respect for your expertise and even for your political views, it seems to me that your answer to the Judge was just riddled with assumptions that may or may not be correct. Let me just give you an example. You said you would expect to see continuing migration if there were continuing bombing or activity, I think is what you said. And that assumes that if a village is completely emptied because of KLA activity or bombing, that you should see people leaving that village later. Well, they can't if they're not there, so that assumption, it seems to me, holds no water if that's the assumption you're making but maybe I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have I misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The position is -- the question is quite clear that people have gone, as you've indicated by the peak, and therefore there can't be another peak. That's the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we estimate there to have been about 875.000 plus or minus some uncertain figure of total refugees who left Kosovo during the period between March and June. There were many more Kosovars before that. Not everybody left. So it is not at all clear to me that these municipalities were completely empty of people; to the contrary, when people returned, I heard anecdotally from many people that there were plenty of people who had never left. So there were people around who could have been conceivably continuing migrants throughout the period if the bombing in fact or the killing were their motivations for leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, for that to make sense you need to look at municipalities as a whole instead of villages and I was talking about villages. Of course within the entire municipality there were people that never left, but some villages were completely emptied of people for one reason or another that we really don't understand at this point I guess and that's the question I'm asking you, not about municipality. So once you've got that peak for a particular village, you're not going to get another one if the people left. That's the point, and it's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it's unfortunately not true because the peak here is not about villages. These peaks are at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think we've beaten this horse to death. Let's go to your second hypothesis. "Air attacks by NATO created local conditions that led to Kosovars being killed and leaving their homes. The NATO influence could either have been direct because people were killed in air-strikes and others fled or indirect because local Yugoslav authorities responded to air-strikes by killing Kosovars and forcing them from their homes." Now, with regard to this hypothesis, again the integrity of your findings depends upon the integrity of your data or the reliability of your data. For instance, if there were air-strikes that coincided with killings or migration that you didn't know about, then your findings could be in error; true?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were lots of air-strikes that spread across the period and linked to periods, then that's possible. However, what we know from adding additional information about air-strikes to this pattern is the reverse and we discussed this at some length yesterday, that most of the air-strikes that occurred occurred in late May and early June. So what's much more likely about air-strikes is that adding data about air-strikes will strengthen the finding here and in fact create the result which I believe to be a coincidence that statistically the implication would be that air-strikes ceased or had a negative effect on killing and migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that was that rather bizarre result that you called a coincidence yesterday where your model found that NATO air-strikes in I think April and May saved lives weeks earlier so you had to reject that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it was not a bizarre result, it was a fairly predictable result which is why we excluded it from our original results. We did not do that calculation in our original report. It's a fairly obvious result if one thinks about the nature of what happens if you have lots of air-strikes later than, in this case, weeks and weeks later than, the killing and migration. The statistical effect of that will be to suggest that there's somehow the killing -- I mean, the air-strikes are suppressing the killing and migration. We don't believe that to be the case, but perhaps -- perhaps someone could argue that. I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll accept that you don't think it's a bizarre result that bombing in April saved lives in March. I think it is. I want to ask you this: You got no data from NATO, did you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got no data from NATO, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You requested no data from NATO?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not request data from NATO, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You did not ask the OTP to get data from NATO for you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You simply relied upon this secondary data that came primarily from, I think you said, a Yugoslav web site and maybe a few other sources?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Principally Yugoslav web sites. I would think that that's actually primary data since the Yugoslav web sites alleged that they were eye-witness accounts. That seems to me primary data.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If NATO had been willing to cooperate with you, if you had even made an effort to get NATO to cooperate with you, and the OTP, they could have told you exactly where they struck, what they struck with, what date, what time, in great detail. They would have that information, and that could be helpful, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably could be if it weren't classified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You never had that data to work with, and I know among other talents you have, one of them is you are a pretty sophisticated computer programmer. You really understand that process pretty well, and so you're certainly well family with the phrase "garbage in and garbage out," aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with it as used inaccurately, yes. It's actually not an appropriate understanding of how statistical analysis works.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, statistical analysis doesn't work at all if you put garbage into the computer you can't expect to get anything but garbage out. Your data has to have some integrity, doesn't it.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. Is your question about my integrity or are you just asserting --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, not your integrity. The data, the data has to be accurate. If you put a bunch of false data in there, then your result is going to be false? Isn't it obvious?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asserting or are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not obvious. Let me explain to you why. Statistical analysis is not about making sausage, as apparently Mr. Ackerman seems to think. Statistical analysis instead is much more like listening to a voice in a crowded, noisy room. You listen to -- you're trying to listen to a voice, concentrate on what the voice is telling you while there are many other voices speaking over you or shouting. Your job as a statistical analyst is to make out the voice that you're trying to hear and then make sense of it. The voice may be speaking softly while others are shouting. It may have a strong accent. I use this metaphor to explain that it is not -- a statistical analysis is, in fact, to the contrary, garbage in garbage out; rather, all statistical -- modern statistical techniques, sometimes called data mining techniques, are about looking at large bodies of information and finding patterns even when there is a lot of chaff mixed in with that data. This notion of garbage in, garbage out, while apparently attractive to people who are not computer programmers, is an inaccurate assessment of the way this work is undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman -- sorry. I don't want to disturb -- carry on. I'll ask the question when you finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that answer is just gobbledygook. You have to agree that if all the data you had was absolutely wrong, then there's no way that you get a result that is meaningful?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If all the data were wrong, that's correct, there would be no meaningful result.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there's a point between all and -- all wrong and all right, where you cross a threshold?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's actually not a point. There's a continuum in which at each point in the continuum where the data are noisier, is the term, as we have more and more chaff, more and more confusing data in the input string, we have a higher and higher error. In fact, that's precisely why statisticians report the error in their results. We do a number of tests - sensitivity analysis is the formal term for these tests - to try to figure out how sensitive our results are to noise or lies or inaccuracies or biases in the data. That's the point of, for example, the entirety of the appendix in the Policy or Panic report. There are a number of sensitivity analyses in the January 2002 report and we spend an enormous amount of effort doing this kind of analysis to ask precisely the question what fraction of the data could be wrong before our results would change. And we have provided extensive analysis to that effect in these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy, you had some kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, I have a vague recollection that somewhere earlier in this case we had figures for NATO strikes, air-strikes in -- used in cross-examination. Do you remember that or is it fantasy on my part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't remember it. I know that there was some data that came from the White Book regarding some NATO air-strikes. I'm not sure that's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I was going to ask you what was the source of that data if you knew it, and it's the White Book, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not able to precisely answer your question. I know there was some data from that, but what apparently the Yugoslav government was compiling there was NATO activity that they considered to be war crimes or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was General Naumann not asked some questions about the extent of NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really would have to look at the transcript. I don't recall, Judge. But I don't think there's any data that ever came from NATO that I'm aware of other than what we can find on the NATO web site. There's some data there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, I was just reminded that at one point I think with General Naumann I'd had some maps that showed NATO bombing,, where the bombs fell and cluster bombs and things of that nature, that were -- a copy was provided to each of you but then you determined that I couldn't use it with General Naumann. Maybe that's what you're thinking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were they a compilation from the White Book?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think they were a compilation based upon data gathered by Yugoslav forces on the ground. That's what I think they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Aleksic is perhaps going to give some guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm now told that data comes from KFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Maybe I would help, Your Honour, I believe that map -- [Interpretation] I believe that's the map where the uranium ammunition used was shown. I think it's the map on which cluster bombs and uranium ammunition were shown, and they were probably obtained from KFOR, because otherwise, we wouldn't have had such data, and part of it was contained in the UN report on uranium ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that wouldn't help on the dates of the bombing; it's information about the results of the bombing, I think. Yeah. Please carry on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, we're not doing a very good job of moving as rapidly as I hoped we could. I'm going to try to avoid some of these highly controversial issues with you, if I can. I want to go to your third hypothesis, and it was: "A systematic campaign by Yugoslav forces drove Kosovar Albanians from their homes and killings were used either to motivate the departures or the killings were a result of the campaign." And if I understand your position correctly, it is that you didn't have sufficient data to draw any conclusions regarding this hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And since your initial report you haven't received sufficient additional data to allow you to draw any conclusions regarding this hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have not continued analysis on this report since 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At paragraph 5.1 of your initial report, then, and I can only give you a K number -- page numbers -- 3831, since I haven't got page numbers on mine for some reason, but it's paragraph 5.1 under the heading: "Kosovo Liberation Army Activity." Are we all there?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's also on the screen. You'll see your description of that activity. "Information on KLA activity was obtained from interview accounts and a variety of non-governmental reports summarised and provided to this project by the ICTY. "Using that information," and this is what I'm really interested in, "the present study counted the number of reported battles between the KLA and Yugoslav forces occurring in each municipality over time." True?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that has not changed -- you wouldn't change that, since this report was issued?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The only other KLA activity to refer to in that paragraph were isolated KLA attacks on Serbs, which didn't figure into your analysis at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Those were a second variable we used to analyse KLA activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. But the primary KLA activity that you analysed was that that involved reported battles between the KLA and Yugoslav forces?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There really wasn't a distinction between primary and secondary, we used them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The conclusion that you drew from this data then is over in the last paragraph of 5.1. "There is no clear cause-and-effect relationship between KLA activity and the pattern described here." Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to do is look at this from a little bit different perspective. If we're talking about data that counts the number of reported battles between KLA and Yugoslav forces occurring in each municipality over time, let's substitute Yugoslav force activity for KLA activity so that when we get to your conclusion we can say: Thus there is no cause-and-effect relationship between Yugoslav force activity and the pattern described here. That would be a fair conclusion from the data, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would be a conclusion if one assumed that the only Yugoslav activity that occurred was that represented by the KLA interactions. It is as if the Yugoslav activity -- the Yugoslavs were not, for example, the authorities in the region, that they did not have police stations throughout the region, it is as if they did not have any defence whatsoever against NATO, it is as if their entire existence can be reduced to this series of conflicts or disappearances committed by the KLA. That seems to me quite a stretch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you don't have any Yugoslav force activity beyond that which is represented by reported battles between KLA and Yugoslav forces occurring in each municipality over time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And therefore we draw no conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, so you can substitute Yugoslav activity for KLA activity?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you get the same place.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't, because doing so requires a massive assumption which you've elided there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think doing so interferes with your assumption that Yugoslav activity might have had some role, although you have no data to indicate it at all. And I think it's extremely fair, since you are relying on clashes between KLA and Yugoslav forces, that you can use either term in the conclusion you get to the same place because you're using the same data. How does that not take sense? You didn't take into account that there were police stations in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He's getting into various statements without giving the witness an opportunity to suggest each --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I haven't noticed that he has any hesitancy to answer me, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd be happy to show hesitancy if you would like, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we're getting into intense debate now, but it seems fairly obvious that what Dr. Ball has been doing in relation to Yugoslav forces is posing a hypothesis and the hypothesis relates to illegal Yugoslav force activity. And as you know, Mr. Ackerman, there's plenty of anecdotal material, on the strength of which I will not comment, to justify starting off with that as one of the hypothesis here. Now, it seems to me there's a clear distinction between looking at that question and looking at the legitimate engagement of the Yugoslav forces with the illegal activity of the KLA, which is the issue that we're addressing at the moment. And I find it difficult to see that there is a way of substituting the Yugoslav force activity of that nature for the KLA activity that was being considered in 5.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you want to explore it more, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to ask questions within the confines of the data that was used by Dr. Ball and what was furnished to him by the Office of the Prosecutor. And that's what he used to draw his conclusions. Now, it may be that there is data outside what he used that maybe could have assisted, that maybe should have been supplied to him by the OTP and wasn't, but it could also be that the OTP had no data that was reliable of independent Yugoslav force activity beyond clashes with the KLA. It seems to me they would have provided that had they had it, and if they had provided it, it seems to me that he would have factored it in. That's my point and I think it's a good one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be but it's a rather different point from the one I think you're making at the moment in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there not a problem with your analysis in that the fact that you limited it to only these three hypotheses which you pretty narrowly constructed. For instance, you made certain assumptions about Kosovar Albanians leaving their homes, when they did it, why they did it -- not necessarily why they did it, but when they did it, how long it took them to get from there to the border. Lots of assumptions were made about that one.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see. As you correctly note, we did not make any assumptions about why they left their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nor did we make assumptions about when they left their homes. We measured when they crossed the border and we looked at the pattern of all people who we could interview in camps who crossed the border on that day and asked those people how long it took them to get to the border. That's not an assumption, that's a model. Models are very useful because they allow us to make a projection within known error. In fact, we devote pages and pages of analysis in the book Policy or Panic to the effect of the model of transit time on the results. Allow me for a moment to review what I mean by transit time because I think it's crucial to the question that's being asked here. This is, I want to emphasise, not an assumption. We went out and asked people in camps, refugee camps: How long did it take you to get to the border? And we knew that people from different parts of Kosovo would take different amounts of time to get to the border. We also knew that some people even leaving the same village would be able to get to the border crossing point relatively quickly, perhaps because they had a vehicle or perhaps because they did not encounter any obstruction along the way, whereas other people trying to get to the border would have a lot of trouble, they would be on foot or they could be on buses that were detained or they could have been detained for other reasons. So we knew there would be a distribution of times that it took to get from people's homes to the border and I'm calling this distribution transit time. We measured the transit time among people in our surveys and we found that for most people they were able to get out in the first day. Over the course of the conflict, the amount of time people spent in transit increased. So if you look at people crossing the border in early March -- excuse me, late March or early April, they're in transit for a relatively short time. If you look at people crossing the border in late April, early May, they're in transit for substantially longer. So what we did with the transit time structure is we said, okay, given people crossing the border on a given day, we know that 50 per cent of them, say, left home today. We know that 20 per cent of them or 30 per cent of them left home yesterday, some smaller fraction left home the day before that and so forth in a declining function. So we took all the people from each village who crossed the border on a given day and we pushed back their date of departure from their homes by the proportion that was shown in the transit time distribution. Now, that's a model and it's an estimate. Consequently, it has error. And so we modelled the error in two different ways. The first way we modelled the error, to see if it would impact our results, was to use the simple sampling error which was the error that resulted because we had taken probability samples of people in refugee camps in order to obtain information about their transit time; actually some of the information was probability sampled, others was not. About -- it was about half and half. The second way, and actually the much more relevant way for this purpose, for this question I think, that we analysed the impact of our transit time analysis is through sensitivity analysis, which I alluded to earlier. And in this case, what we did is think about all the factors that shape the transit time distribution and we identified six different factors that affect how long it would take people, statistical factors that would affect the structure of how long it would take people to get to the border. We varied all of those factors to what we found extreme positive and negative values and recalculated the migration analysis, and we found - and you will find if you look in appendix 1 of Policy or Panic - that the transit time assumptions have almost no impact on the conclusions that we draw about the process of migration, either looking overall, looking at all of Kosovo, or looking at any of the four regions that we identify, north, south, east, and west. So let me be very clear with Mr. Ackerman that this is not an assumption, but rather, a model and an analysis that we spent quite a few weeks examining from many different angles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, is Policy or Panic an exhibit in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, let me -- I didn't mean to get such a long answer from you. Most of it you gave us -- most of it's an answer you gave us yesterday, but let me see if I can talk about an assumption that you will agree that you made. I think it's the case that you made an assumption that if NATO bombing occurred after, significantly after, like four days I think is your number, four days after people left the village, then the NATO bombing was not a factor in their leaving?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. We're going back into the peaks and troughs analysis here, Mr. Ackerman, and I would hate to repeat my reservations with that analysis again. Instead, let me say that our analysis rejecting the hypotheses of NATO and KLA activity being plausible causes of killing and migration rest on the residuals analysis which is in the original report figures 10 and 11 of which, as far as I can tell, not a question has been raised. Now, I will -- I'm happy if it pleases the Bench to repeat my reservations, but since you have just complained that I repeated my correction of your inaccurate characterisation of our work as an assumption, you then complained that I had to correct you at some length because of your failure to understand what I said yesterday. I would hate to do that again unless that would please the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really don't think you need to say it again if you said it yesterday. That's up to the Chamber, if they want to hear it again or not. I suspect they don't. You will agree that people can't act on information if it's not communicated to them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the converse of that is true. So if people live in a village, for instance, just as a for instance, if people live in a village that has a Yugoslavia army barracks in that village and the information that's communicated to them is that NATO is bombing Yugoslav Army installations, it seems to me they must consider that information and one of the things they may decide to do based upon that information is leave the village. If that installation -- and they did that, they left the village. If that installation was then bombed, say, ten days later, your conclusion would be that the NATO bombing had absolutely no effect on their leaving the village, when in fact that was exactly the reason why they left the village; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion would be that the NATO bombing of the village had no effect on their leaving. My work is not an analysis of the psychology of rumour, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about rumour, I'm talking about a hypothetical situation that I think probably has a lot of basis in reality with regard to what happened on the ground in Kosovo. You need to understand what we're not doing here is some kind of an academic exploration of statistical methods; what we're doing here is deciding whether or not there is sufficient information available to this Court that would allow them to find beyond a reasonable doubt that certain matters alleged in the indictment in this case is true. And I think one of the things we're all having difficulty with is where -- you've made it very clear, I think, that at best your conclusions don't prove anything. I think you've used those exact words, that they don't prove anything.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My work disproves two hypotheses that may be relevant to the Court; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you want to go as far as disprove either because disproving is proving?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's sophistry, Mr. Ackerman. We are quite clear in our analysis that we reject the hypotheses that either KLA or NATO activity could have been the causes of killing or migration. I will not play with the words that you've tossed out there. That's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you, just for instance, did you look at the Kosovo media, television, radio, newspapers, to see what kind of information was being transmitted to the people in the villages regarding what might happen next in their lives? Did you look at that to see if you could see if that had any effect on whether or not they might have left their villages?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This analysis is neither an analysis of the psychology of rumour or of propaganda, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you want to refer to it as rumour and propaganda, you can. But what if NATO or what if KLA or what if Yugoslav forces were actually warning villagers that there was going to be a battle in their village and based on that warning, they appropriately left that village. I mean, we have some information in this case that that was the case. That's not rumour; that's reality. And you're ignoring reality, it seems to me, in your report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's pop back to reality then, Mr. Ackerman. It may be a refreshment. In figure 2 of my original report, page 6, we show a comparison of people leaving their homes for whatever reason and people being killed. If we then -- you'll notice that those two curves are very similar and I can provide statistical descriptions of that similarity that show that they are actually extremely similar patterns. Similarly, figures 4, 5, 6, and 7 show the same pattern broken down by region. If people were leaving their homes as a result of the rumours that Mr. Ackerman alludes to, it fails to explain why they were being killed at precisely the same times and same places, unless perhaps Mr. Ackerman knows something about the potential fatality of newspapers which has eluded us. My explanation of these two patterns coinciding so very closely in time and space is that, in fact, there is a common cause to both, and it is highly unlikely to me that it is newspapers or any other -- a rumour or anything else; rather, something that I believe we can agree that a killing is a violent act, so there is something violent going on that is creating the pattern of migration and killing, creating both, because it is very difficult to explain how we would have such close patterns in time and space without a common cause. Because we interpret the likely cause as a violent one, we focussed our hypotheses on those parties able to deploy violence in the conflict; hence, the three hypotheses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In relation to your findings, where you that - and I'm looking at figure 8 and the analysis related to figure 8 in your original report - where you say that in 11 of the 29 municipalities, KLA activity coincided with the overall peak and we were to -- and we were to be looking at only these municipalities, because that's -- the indictment's divided into municipalities. I know that's not what you're looking at at the moment, but let's assume that these were the 11 municipalities that we were looking at in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What would your conclusion be in relation to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would depend on what happened at moments other than the peaks, sir. So if the -- there might be a coincidence of KLA activity, for example, and killing in a particular municipality at the peak of that killing, but if there were continuing KLA activity throughout the rest of the period without there being killing, we would have to ask the question: Well, what's happening with the KLA activity then? This gets back to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can find that in here in relation to each individual municipality, can we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There are 29 graphs in the report that I presented in the January 2007 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, and that will deal with it for every separate municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All four series are on those graphs, and I'm happy to present them in other formats if it would please the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And one of the important ones, just as an example, is Pristina --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- and your conclusion about Pristina is that it's not consistent with the overall view that you have of Kosovo in general. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pristina is a special case, because it is the site of an overwhelming amount of NATO and KLA activity, being the capital. Let me pull up that graph. Let's see. Page 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's page 19.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Pristina. Yeah. So you can see that Pristina was the target of an almost daily bombing campaign throughout the period of analysis here. But the peaks occur at the very beginning and then again in mid-April. So, you know, there's bombing every single day; yet there's migration only at specific moments. Why would -- you know, why would there be migration on some days and not on others if there's bombing every day? I mean, I think that would be my principal question about this relationship. The -- you know, in particular you can see that there's a continuous bombing pattern toward the later period after the 7th of April or so, or the 10th of April, it seems, whereas the peak of migration comes right at the beginning of the conflict where there's also bombing. This is Pristina. There's bombing there continuously. So the causality would require, it seems to me, having both a positive correlation, which is what this analysis of peaks would do, saying that there is bombing and migration, or KLA attacks and killing, but there must also be the negative correlation. There must also be the absence of the two that coincide together, so that if one is present and the neither is not, neither is the other present. I think an interesting case that may bring this up is -- let me scroll backward. An interesting municipality to this effect is -- yeah -- yeah, is back to Djakovica where we have a single air-strike and a single KLA action and then a very extensive amount of migration and a fairly large number of killings and then a nearly continuously pattern or a fairly regular pattern, at minimum, of bombing and of KLA activity that is not -- that does not correspond with subsequent killing and migration. So I mean, if we contrast Djakovica and Pristina, we get at this sense of things must vary in both directions, not simply in one. Does that assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm trying to understand at the moment is in relation to a municipality where you cannot make the finding that what happened is inconsistent with KLA activity --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- what do we do about that? I mean, we can look at that as a separate municipality and say: We've got no assistance there in identifying support for perhaps oral evidence that we've heard about the cause of people moving. I mean, we can't just look at this as a blanket exercise for the whole of Kosovo when we have an indictment related to individual parts of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir. I think that the -- the purpose of a statistical analysis is -- well, and, really, its limitation is this big-picture approach. It is quite difficult to use a statistical analysis of this kind to look at individual cases the way the indictment is written. Instead, this may be understood as a kind of broad picture where broad explanations might be tested. I'm afraid that -- I'm afraid that the method does not easily permit very, very small-scale or focussed findings of the kind that you've requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Some time ago in answer to my last question about media, you said something about newspapers and you used the term -- you used the phrase: It seems highly unlikely to me. It was back a page or so ago when you were answering that question about the possible effect of newspaper coverage. The term "highly unlikely" is not a statistical term of art, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this case, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. And so when you used the term "it's highly unlikely to me," you were not being a scientist but an advocate for a position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was being a scientist trying to explain something to a non-scientist, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman, that's about two hours you've had, and we have a stream of counsel behind you. We have to be realistic about how we approach this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very aware that I'm basically out of time. I was hoping to get through a lot more material in the time available, and as you saw, we got bogged down in some pretty technical things and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I express the concern I had yesterday. Is anyone going to be cross-examining on the basis of a competing expert report, which is the sort of assistance, I think, we would particularly welcome rather than the sort of common-sense question that might occur to any of us but isn't terribly well-founded, perhaps, as a way of challenging the exercise that's being conducted here. So you see if the cross-examination was of the latter type, then it could go on forever. I could think of questions to ask interminably about this from a common-sense point of view, but they may be matters for argument rather than matters on which Dr. Ball can comment. I'd much rather hear cross-examination that focused on the expertise he's used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to try to finish in ten minutes. I may not be able to, because Dr. Ball may have to go into further long explanations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think what we should do is come back to you if we have time, Mr. Ackerman. It think you've had a fair crack of the whip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm willing to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only other thing I'm conscious of doing is interrupting your question about the comparison between KLA in conflict with Yugoslav forces and Yugoslav forces in conflict with KLA, and I may have been premature in interrupting you on that, and if you do want to explore that further, that would help, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were suggesting that the same conclusion ought to be drawn in relation to Yugoslav forces on the basis of the data that were available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's clarity in the report, and I think anything further I would do with it would be, as you have pointed out, more in the nature of argument than of a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think we should --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would be happy to yield to my colleagues, and if there is some more time at the end, I actually do have some more questions I would like to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try and be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may go ahead and laugh if I ask a layman's question, because I've no idea about statistics whatsoever. What I wanted to ask you about differs from the cross-examination so far. If I understood properly, Mr. Ball -- but first of all, my name is Toma Fila and I appear on behalf of Mr. Sainovic here. In the report you compiled on the 3rd of January 2002, it is entitled "Killings and Refugee Flow in Kosovo between March and June 1999." What I'm interested in is -- out of everything I've read is the following: I saw that the report was not ordered or financed by the OTP, but you nevertheless sent it to them. I'm interested in the title itself. Who ascribed that title to the report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You did. I'm asking you this because when one looks at the title, one is bound to conclude that this concerns movements of Kosovo population; however, if you read through it - and you will agree, I presume - one comes to the conclusion that it concerns itself only with Albanians. Therefore, the question is this: Did you try to ignore -- or perhaps to put it this way. We heard Ms. Sandra Mitchell on the 11th of July before this Chamber. It was page 565 and 566, lines 20 to 25 and 1 to 7, if I'm not mistaken, since I don't have my glasses on. She confirmed the findings of the UNHCR from Geneva of the 15th of October in 1999, whereby on that occasion during the NATO air campaign over 100.000 Serbs left Kosovo. Do you accept such data? If not, I can hand you the report itself.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there's such a report. I have not studied it, so I'm not competent to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No comments. I just wanted to see whether you are willing to accept such information. Second of all, if you're familiar with the whole thing, you will agree that apart from the Albanians, who were the most numerous and the Serbs, there were other ethnicities whose members also fled Kosovo and the war. My question, hence, is the following: Why didn't you mention in the title that this concerns killings and refugee flow of Albanian population in Kosovo? Otherwise, one is given the impression that there were no others or that you found it unimportant for them as to why they had fled Kosovo. It was not in dispute that they indeed fled Kosovo. Wouldn't it be more scientific to analyse all 29 municipalities out of which some were purely Serb, some purely Albanian, and others were mixed, to see what the attitude was of the population to the bombs that were being dropped on their heads, but to focus also on the population which was not Serb. And then to have an overall picture of the impact of those bombs on the general population of Kosovo. That was my question. And again, I apologise for putting it in lay terms.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No apology necessary. I think the essence of a scientific analysis is to pick a sufficiently focused question so that we can address it. I think it would be very interesting to conduct a study analysing the patterns of migration and killing among the various other ethnicities in Albania during this -- excuse me, in Kosovo during this time. We chose, as you noted, to focus on the most numerous group, the Kosovar Albanians. But that certainly would not exclude any study done of other groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You will agree, I believe, that if you applied the three hypotheses to the other peoples who also fled, you would probably come up with different conclusions as to why they had fled. Probably their reasons would be different to those of the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't studied those groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Another thing on the topic. You said that you went to only one single border crossing, and perhaps this will be examined in more detail by my colleagues. In the Milosevic trial where you testified on the 28th of February 2005, there was a testimony by a doctor, a physician, Dr. Aleksovski from Macedonia who received the refugees who crossed the border over to Macedonia. He confirmed that the Albanian refugees stated that they were fleeing from the NATO campaign, which is different from what you have been telling us. And I hope that we will have that person here as a witness but I wanted to ask you this and his transcript is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were hundreds of thousands of Albanian refugees, perhaps 875.000 plus or minus a very large number. I'm not sure of the error around that figure. Certainly some of them may have said some things, such as what you suggest. However, my study is not concerned with what people said they did, but rather with the sequence of events which may have motivated their departures. This is not a study of attitude or of people's reports about why they did something, but rather the timing of the events in their area and then their subsequent killing or departure, their being killed or departing, leaving for Albania or for Macedonia, Bosnia, or for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. I wanted to tell you something else. In your report you mentioned a unilateral cease-fire that was put in force by Yugoslavia on the 6th of April, 1999. You said that the cease-fire was not respected by either NATO or the KLA. It was Easter, it was Orthodox Easter. Quite the contrary, they stepped-up their activity. It can be read from your report that the Serbs did not fire their weapons at that time. What I will put to you is that they did because we refused to cease protecting the Serbs because someone was opening fire at them. How would this fit in with your report? If someone's opening fire at the Army of Yugoslavia, of course they're not going to just sit around and wait.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowhere in my report do I say that the Serbs did not fire their weapons. What I said is that the government of Yugoslavia announced on television that there would be a cease-fire. Whether or not that cease-fire was respected on the ground, I don't know. What I do know is that immediately after the cease-fire, the number of reported killings and migrations drops very low relative to its earlier period. That's the observation that we make when we say that there is a strong coincidence between the session of stated hostilities by the Yugoslav government and killing and migration. It's whether or not the hostilities actually ceased; that's beyond this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is not in the electronic system, therefore I cannot put this before you in that way. But unless the OTP objects, I can show you this and it shows the flow of refugees. You can even keep it if you wish to. You can use it as evidence later on. This is one of OTP's documents. This would actually conclude my cross-examination, since I wouldn't be allowed to use this, I believe. But just one more question of a more general nature. Of course you need not know necessarily about it and I'll try and explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Fila, what's going on here? Why are you handing this over?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I cannot use it, I just wanted to hand it over. They can keep it and the witness can keep it. One can see the migration patterns. It wasn't in the system, therefore I cannot use it but the OTP may well use it if they want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Last year there was a committee of the National Assembly formed and some people were sent down to Kosovo. Together with Albanian representatives they compiled a report, an overview, of all those missing and killed. The figure is about 9.700, out of which some 4.000 are Albanians and some 3.000 Serbs as well as others. I have their findings here, although untranslated. I intended to use it later. In total it was less than 10.000 of all groups. They counted every single head. Later on when I will be allowed to use that, if I were able to show it to you now, would it change your views that the total figure is not the one you estimated? And there were only slightly over 4.000 Albanians killed or missing. Even Ms. Natasa Kandic who cooperates with the Prosecutor's office agrees with the figures. Would that have an impact on your findings or thoughts on that? Of course, I'm not trying to enter into any polemics about whether it should or not, but I'm simply asking whether it would.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's separate the question. There's really two different questions here. The first question is how many people -- how many Kosovar Albanians were killed. And my experience over many years is that no many how many times you try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've told us this yesterday. That's not the question, Dr. Ball. The question is: Assume for the moment that slightly over 4.000 Albanians were killed and that figure was accurate --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- let's assume that. What difference does that make to your conclusions? That's Mr. Fila's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If those people are distributed in the same way that we have shown in, for example, figure 1 of appendix 3 of my January 2002 report it will make no impact at all on our analysis. The analysis will be the same. Our analysis does not rest on the total magnitude of deaths; it rests on the distribution of those deaths across time and space.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the figure wouldn't change your opinion? You dealt with the topic extensively, even during the Milosevic trial, but I failed to understand and I fail to understand now. To move on to a third thing, to a third topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please bring it up in e-court. It is table 1, page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your report of the 28th of January, 2007, the 29 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still don't have it. It is Exhibit P2678. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I tried to do some math with this, and if I was incorrect, I apologise again. If we follow the columns, can you please count the number of coincides to establish the number of municipalities in which there was a coincidence of KLA and NATO actions with killing and migration. You can use the electronic pen and I will give you my figure so as to be able to compare that to yours. KLA activity coincided in nine municipalities, whereas NATO activity in six.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be happy to do this; however, I'm afraid that we're going to go into the same area of discussion that Mr. Ackerman and I covered at some length about this method. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So here we go. So you want me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ball, in my country, we do not tend to repeat. You only repeat if there was a lot of noise in the communication channel, but I do not think we have that and I do not intend to follow Mr. Ackerman's line of questioning. And since we're not deaf, either of us, I guess we may pursue. Therefore, in nine municipalities we had coincidences of NATO activity -- sorry, KLA activity and in six municipalities NATO activity. And in Djakovica, Pec, and Pristina we have both NATO and KLA activity. Am I correct in thinking that in 12 municipalities the murders coincided with KLA and/or NATO activity?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's what you put in.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, sir. The -- what coincides is the single greatest day, the peak of killing and migration. That is quite different than saying that the entirety coincides. So again, as I said to Mr. Ackerman, in order for us to make the conclusion that there is, as you just said, that the murders coincide more broadly, we would have to find both the positive and the negative correlation. We would have to find an absence of KLA --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that. I understand that. That's why I said we shouldn't repeat twice. I'm counting your coincidences or the number of the word and I'm trying to put it in figures so as to reflect the table. When we are discussing migration - and you can count to see whether I'm telling the truth - I'm telling you that in ten municipalities migration coincided with KLA activity; that's what you put into the table. And in nine municipalities, migration coincided with NATO bombardment. Since in the municipalities of Orahovac, Pec, and Pristina, as well as Prizren, migration coincided with both KLA and NATO activity, may we conclude therefore that in 15 municipalities migration coincided with either KLA or NATO activity or both? This is simply what I'm reading out of the table. A sample yes or no would do.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply have to correct the identification of what you're claiming coincides. What coincides again is not activity in a general sense; what coincides is the peak of activity. Okay. So there's maybe activity -- there may be killing and migration at other times -- but this is quite an important distinction, sir, so I want to make sure that it's included in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. But the figures I stated are correct; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without checking them, they seem roughly correct, yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that out of the total of 29 municipalities, the word "coincidence," whether it reflects the peaks or totality, killings and migration coincide to a large degree with - if I may have a moment - the figure is quite a high one, having in mind the total of 29 municipalities, and we come up with the number of 15 more or less, 15 out of 29. If we know - and I believe we do - that the municipalities of Zvecan, Leposavic, Strpce and Novo Brdo are almost purely Serb ethnically speaking and you said that the four Albanians -- the total of Albanians that were there left and if we say that these are purely ethnically Serbian places as well as the municipality of Gora, where there are Albanians who speak Serbian, then the importance or the weight of the conclusion is even greater because those municipalities need to be extracted out of the group. And you discussed this with Mr. Ackerman, and I just wanted to add something and that is in the municipalities relevant to the indictment there are two or more coincidences. And for Pristina there is a coincidence in all four categories, which means that killings and migration coincided with the activity of both KLA and NATO, and you confirmed that in your text at page 4 and of the second paragraph in the English. Is that correct? Do you stand by what you put in that text?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I put in the text; however, I am concerned that you are over-interpreting the coincidence. The coincidence must be understood only as a coincidence because if we were --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That was my understanding of it, yes, that's what you said to Mr. Ackerman. Yes. But the coincidence is there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The importance of the coincidences is that they remain in a minority of municipalities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily, sir. Even -- as I said before, even if we had coincidences in every single one of these cells, the causal argument would still be undermined if there were bombings when there was no migration, if there were KLA attacks when there was no killing. You see, the problem with this coincidence argument is that it only observes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where I'm struggling - I'm obviously not understanding something here - but I understood that where there was a minority of coincidence -- of municipalities where there was a coincidence, that you could say that the activity you were investigating, for example, bombing, was not consistent with the idea that that caused the movement or the killings -- the movement of people. Now, are you saying that that's a wrong understanding of your report, that the minority is not significant in coming to that conclusion, that negative conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The minority would lead to that conclusion, but the converse is not true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what Mr. Fila now is identifying - and all the names have not come up on the transcript, Mr. Fila, so perhaps you can tell us which of the municipalities in brackets are you saying are purely or principally Serb populated? I think you said Gora was one --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Gora is a municipality where the Gorani live. These are people who speak the Serbian language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but they are Muslims. They are not Albanians, they are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... was one?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zvecan, Leposavic, Strpce, Novo Brdo. Let me do it again. Zvecan, Leposavic, Strpce, Novo Brdo, and Gora. Is it wrong again? Oh, yes, and Zubin Potok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, there are six municipalities where it's suggested that there's no significant Albanian population to be affected by this. Now, is that of some importance in analysing your statistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this is -- I would suggest that this -- while this table provides rich fodder for debate about specific places, I think that the statistical analysis should be -- that the statistical finding should be made on the basis of figures 10 and 11 in the original report, where a much more thorough statistical test of these relationships is made, Your Honour.
