That I really -- I must say that we've -- it is unfortunate that we've focused so much on this because the real analysis is in those two figures and that -- those are the two figures that show a proper statistical test of the relationships among four simultaneous variables. It's quite complex to look at a table like this and choose a single day form each -- or single two-day period in fact from each of these 29 municipalities and treat that single two-day period as though it is determinant of the history of the conflict in that region. So I would urge us to look at a more consistent and a more thorough test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even though these -- when you look at table 1 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and you look at these municipalities mentioned, they are the ones where all along the row no prior -- no inconclusive -- I think no prior in fact is the finding --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. There are others, too, as well. Kosovo Polje, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If there aren't people there who are likely to be moved by Serb forces, does that not tend to have an impact on the overall significance of looking at 29 municipalities --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- when six of them are populated by people to whom your third hypothesis would not apply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but an inverse-thought hypothesis might apply which is that if we were to assume - which my study does not - if we were to assume that the cause of killing and migration were the Yugoslav authorities, and if we were to assume that Yugoslav authorities were not killing or forcing Serb populations to move, then we would in fact find precisely the patterns in the Serb-dominant municipalities that we find here. So although it had not occurred to us and it is outside the realm of our report, the observations that have been made by counsel confirm or would tend to confirm the claim that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. First of all, I wasn't the person who chose this table; it's your table. I'm not the one who made it. Secondly, could you please do what it was that I asked you to do. First answer a question that I have for you. Kosovo is a relatively small territory. You come from America. It is so small for you. It's small from the point of view of my country let alone yours. So let's assume that these municipalities are not islands. It's not Indonesia is it? These are villages that are nearby to each other. So isn't it logical to assume that panic and fear spread and that migrants spread this and that it has a hallow effect, you know, it's when libel starts, you don't know who even started it. So that is how it spreads. And if we were to look at this spiral, now how should I put this, rumours spread and people move out as a matter of inertia especially from mixed communities. Albanians see that Serbs are fleeing, Serbs see that Albanians are fleeing. All of them together see that the Gorani are fleeing.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This panic spreads among these municipalities. Now, did you take into account that effect? You know, the bombing is an ongoing process. The document that the Prosecutor did not give you, I am so sorry about that, because there is this review of when who left but they didn't want to give you the document so there. You see people are leaving all the time at different points at time. You only looked at Albanians; we looked at others as well. So in the question of intrigue, this is called the hallow effect, but I mean here it is panic that spreads especially in such a community like Kosovo is. Now what am I trying to say. It is not that the three hypotheses are the only causes, the one that you mentioned, it's panic, too, fear.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the question is, did we take into account panic, I repeat my earlier answer that this is not a study of psychology of war or rumour. We took into account simply the movements of people and the actions of the KLA and NATO and killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Now, in order to check my conclusions, could you use your own pen on this graph that is right in front of you and mark the numbers that I mentioned to you so that this could become an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's useful. We've got the figures, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine. No problem. Right. Thank you. That would be all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have questions, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you guide us on the timing?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope it would be very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think what we'll do is come back at 10 past -- in fact, we'll come back at quarter past and you can start at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll have to have a break now, Dr. Ball. The usher will take you again and you will leave the courtroom and we'll see you at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Ball. I am Branko Lukic, and I have only a few questions for you. In your introductory section in paragraph 2, you say: "Nothing contained in this publication should be considered legal advice for concrete cases. This publication like all formulations and positions contained herein are only meant for information purposes." Nevertheless, we believe that in your findings you do give a opinion and you draw some conclusions and you even give legal opinions, albeit unintentionally perhaps. For example, you say that in the questions that you dealt with there were killings involved. I would like to ask you the following. In your findings, did you take into -- a single category all fatalities, civilian deaths, killings of KLA fighters, Albanians who were killed by the KLA, as well as people who died of natural causes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We included in our analysis only those deaths that occurred by violence, that occurred during the period of the study. We do not know who killed the people, and in fact the inferences about who killed the people are the basis for the hypotheses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that all the information you published was published in the following way. You protected the privacy of the persons involved and that all the data you published actually do not contain any personal identification of the victims or the witnesses of these events?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the Defence has no possibility of checking this information. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's a matter which is outside of the competence of the witness. The Prosecution did disclose to the Defence over a period of years the supporting material that was used or the source material that was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Including the identity of all the victims?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's the question he's asking. Which is a perfectly legitimate question for him to ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of this witness -- very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If the witness can't answer it, he'll tell us he can't answer it. He's a perfectly sensible person when it comes to knowing his limitations. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ball, can you answer this question, please?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm limited by not knowing precisely what the OTP has disclosed to the Defence. If the OTP disclosed to the Defence the original statements and interviews that were conducted by the groups that provided data to us for our analysis, then you should have all the victims' names unless those names have been redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. I was incorrect. The disclosure did include the names of the victims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the answer is: Yes, you do have all those names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ball, in terms of evidence supporting your report, we have officially been provided with one document, P3193. That is one of the 690 reports you collected at the Morina border crossing and we did not receive anything else officially from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Lukic, that must be wrong. You're distinguishing between what's an exhibit in the case, I think, and the disclosure. The Prosecution position is that they have disclosed it all to you but it's not exhibited. Now, are you disputing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, I'm not aware of -- we had the discussions during the cross-examination of Mr. Abrahams and Ms. Mitchell, and I'm not aware that we received all those statements disclosed. So -- but I wouldn't bother this witness with this. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is something you obviously can take up with the OTP and raise with us also if, in fact, our understanding is inaccurate. I would just like to ask one question, though. Mr. Lukic touched initially there on something which may be of some importance. The KLA are said on occasions to have killed Albanians who were perhaps collaborators or seen to have official positions or whatever. In your hypothesis in relating to activity of the KLA, you confine it to the KLA ordering people to leave or because people fled fighting between KLA and Yugoslav forces, which seems to leave out of account discrete acts of murder that may have been committed against individuals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct; however, you are also correct that if the KLA were to have conducted executions in the style you suggest, they would also have been included in that hypothesis. The same logic would be obtained. Any KLA killing directly or indirectly would have been cover by that hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic mentioned a number that I think may have caused -- flags for me that there may be a little bit of confusion I can clear up. He said he has only one of 690 pages. I think the 690 pages refer to the Albanian border documents that were disclosed to the Milosevic court - I don't know if they have been disclosed here - but they are distinct from the Human Rights Watch and OSCE materials which were the subject of the exchange with Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you may have -- oh, yes, it is. It's P1393 and it is one of the documents taken from the border post, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today on page 37, line 12, in response to a question you said that you did not care about what people say. It had to do with what Albanians crossing the border said. However, was that not precisely your own source of information, what people were saying as they were crossing the border, in relation to when it was that they had left their homes and when they were crossing the border?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am interested in when people said they left their homes. I'm interested in when they crossed the border. I am not interested - and we did not ask - why people left their homes, nor what their fears were or any other of the psychological discussions that surrounded the conversation to which you allude.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that soon. Do you know, since foreigners did not speak Albanian, that the interpreters who were interpreting for the foreigners there were primarily from the Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms, who were Albanians themselves?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms, I believe, conducted some translations, but certainly not for all four of the projects. I believe they did for two of the four original projects, and it is not my understanding they had anything to do with the three recent projects we have just used in the January 2007 report. So perhaps two of the seven data sources used for the analysis of killings were related to the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which two, I think we should be clear about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I believe for the ABA/CEELI data, and I think there may have been - and here I'm remembering perhaps an error - that there were some translators for the OSCE that may have been from the Council For the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms. That can be confirmed with OSCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members of this council were at the same time members of the KLA, often very highly positioned in the ranks of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Several times today you pointed out that you were not interested in psychology but that you were dealing with statistics; however, I would like to ask you precisely about the psychological part of your findings. Actually, you took two days at a time, that is to say, two days prior to the peaks of killings or of departures that people feared NATO bombings only two days prior to -- or rather, after the bombing itself. So could you kindly explain to the honourable Trial Chamber and to me on the basis of what do you reach these findings? How come you took only these two-day periods?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, we used two-day periods throughout the analysis because the amount of data available to us was inadequate to do day-by-day analysis. So we cumulated each pair of days together in order to do the analysis. There simply wasn't enough information to do consistent analysis in single days. Second, I think what you refer to in your question is that in the analysis of peaks and troughs, particularly peaks, which we have been over at some length this morning and is captured most clearly in the table we've been debating, which I don't have at hand but which is the one that discusses coincidences no prior or inconclusiveness, that to define a peak of killing or migration as coinciding with KLA activity or bombing, we used four days prior to the bombing or the -- or the KLA activity in order to determine whether or not the event were to coincide with the peak. So it's not a two-day period, it's a four-day period. We chose four days because that seemed to us a reasonable period of time for people to react to a specific event. If the event were longer, it would be classified as inconclusive, and in fact we provide in the new report that the January 27 report -- January 28th, sorry, 2007 report, we provide a fairly extensive analysis of these inconclusives. And inconclusive in this context is a municipality in which the air-strike or the KLA activity occurred more than four days prior to the peak of killing or migration. So if you prefer a longer period, if you wish to make an argument about a longer period, then the graphs -- the 29 graphs in that report and the analysis of inconclusives can provide you with material to make such an argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that in documentation or literature from psychiatry or psychology you did not find a base for such calculations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 20th and 21st of March, 1999, there were convoys of refugees, and we heard about them from an Albanian witness who testified here, that was prior to the bombing. How would they fit into your analyses before the fighting and during the stay of the verifiers in Kosovo? Can you somehow fit that into your own analysis?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our analysis starts later than that period, precisely because that's before the Albanian border guards began systematically recording people crossing the border, neither did OSCE or UNHCR have systematic and rigorous counting going on at that time. However, let's keep in mind that our argument is that it is unlikely that the -- in fact, we've rejected the hypothesis that the bombing is the cause of refugee flow. So the fact that there were -- that there was extensive refugee flow before the bombing is perfectly consistent with our broader claim. If there were convoys of refugees before the bombing, clearly the bombing did not cause those convoys of refugees to be on the move. That's similar to what we see throughout the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But can we conclude that that is not in accordance with your own conclusion, that people were leaving only because their particular region was under attack? Is this not along the lines of what my learned friend Mr. Fila said, that fear cannot be confined so narrowly? Fear can exist without direct attacks and that one has to have a broader view than you had in your own tables.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a somewhat complicated statement. Let me see if I can unpack it. The claim is that the convoy of people that's moving before the bombing are moving from fear. I have no idea why they're moving. This is not an analysis of psychology. What is clear, and what I think we can all agree on, is that these people are certainly not moving because their region has been bombed. That's the point of our analysis. If the bombing has not started, then clearly the bombing has not motivated them to start. If we want to speculate about the psychological state of these people, then -- well, I suppose that speculation is possible but I do not engage in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that at that time there weren't any attacks by Serb forces either because verifiers were in Kosovo and they never reported about any such attacks?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's true or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's beyond the competence of the witness, that question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 15 in the English, paragraph 2, you say: "The statistical analysis of correlation cannot prove that the Yugoslav forces were the external factor responsible for the patterns observed." It is item 5.4, Yugoslav forces, the first paragraph. Do you abide by that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 15, paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] 5.4, Yugoslav forces, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. That's correct. We are clear throughout the report that we do not make affirmative proofs in this report or in any of the various addenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right below you state: "However, the findings of this study are in keeping with the hypothesis that the activity of the Yugoslav forces was the cause of murders and migration of refugees." My question, hence, is this: If you weren't able to conclude that based on statistical analysis of correlation, based on what did you make your conclusions as a statistician?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you follow in the next paragraph after the one you've read, we observe a circumstantial link between the cease-fire of the 6th and 7th of April and the decline of killings and migration. That is the basis for our observation that the evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that Yugoslav forces were responsible for killing and migration. This is not proof, but it is an interesting circumstantial link.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the last sentence of the very -- paragraph you say: "Further connection or links can be established if it can be proven that the movement of Yugoslav troops followed the same pattern as the cases of killings and refugee flow; however, such analysis would lie outside the scope of the study." Therefore, you did not investigate or study that any further since it went out of the scope of your study?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 45, paragraph 5 in the English, item 3, 3.3, aggregation of cross-checked tables to explain, or rather, aggregation of the cross-classification tables to account for sparseness.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you say: "The next goal for this analysis is the estimation of the number of killings for each of 192 space time points representing 48 two-day time-periods and four geographical regions." Who determined this to be a goal, you or the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues and I did, my co-authors and I did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 47, second paragraph, figure 7. "Counts of zero cells for the four-way tables." You say: "Collapsing to the 24 four-day periods over the four regions yields 96 cross-classification tables. Of these, 48 or 50 per cent contain more than ten zeros. Collapsing to the 16 six-day periods over the four regions yields 64 cross-classification tables. Of these, 26 or 41 per cent contain more than ten zeros. Collapsing further will impede the analysis desired." However, we heard that you collapsed that to two days. Did that impede the analysis desired?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we are doing the analysis over the entire region, we do it by two-day periods. The migration analysis -- the stuff we're talking about here in this appendix that you've just referred to exclusively treats the killing analysis. The migration analysis, first to set aside, was done exclusively in two-day periods by municipality that were then aggregated to regions. This analysis on killings was done in a slightly more complex way because the data is -- there's less of it, it's thinner. So we did the analysis for the entire period -- excuse me, for the entire region by two-day period and then we -- if you'll follow into the next paragraph, we found that we could do, instead of four-way cross-classification tables, we could do three-way cross-classification tables and then do each combination, each possible combination. If we have four systems, you can create four possible combinations of three systems. So we have four data sets, now we have seven, but then we had four, and we could create them by saying we'll take A, B, and C or A, B, and D or any possible combination you can draw, four possible combinations of three sets from four possible sets. And what we did is find that by doing so, as we explain in the subsequent narrative, we could make much more finally grained estimates than we could by approaching it at the top level using four-way classification systems. So this is an explanation of why we chose to use the three-at-a-time method.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, your explanation is that this did not impede the analysis desired or it did?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's right --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] My mistake.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not impede. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 57, paragraph 4, you state: "The regression models using migrations as the dependent variable, however, yield a different interpretation. In this case there appears to be an association between KLA activities and migrations, specifically the association between KLA battles within the previous time-period and migrations in the current time-period appears to be significant. The R square for both of these models are high, further confirming an association." Can we say that the KLA, or rather, their activities had any impact on migration?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we're finding here is that there's some association. What we continue -- and if you continue looking through on to page 59 where we make our final conclusions with that, we are observing that there are some statistical associations but that those statistical associations are insufficient to change the underlying patterns of the migration and killing. Figures 20 and 21 give you the detail on that. In particular - and I appreciate you raising this, because this is, in fact, the core of our causal argument about how this -- how these relationships work. The statistical analysis finds that there is some relationship between KLA patterns and NATO patterns; however, once one controls for those relationships, once we remove the statistical effect of the relationships between the KLA and NATO activity and killings and migration, we find that the patterns of killing and migration remain substantively unchanged and that the -- the lack of change is shown quite clearly in the eight graphs shown in figures 21 and -- 20 and 21, pages 59 and 60. If I may explain one, perhaps, they're a bit confusing. If -- would it help the Bench if I explained one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you think so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So if we consider figure 20 on page 59. Figure 20 is titled: "Estimated Total Killings and Residuals by Region Over Time," and these are the graphs that result from the statistical coefficients shown in figure 19 in the second column. The effect of this graph, to start out is -- well, the meaning of this graph is, first, that the dark black lines in each of the four graphs show the estimated total killings for that region, the total number of killings that we believe to have occurred, given our four sources and given the adjustment that we've made for the under-reporting bias which we believe to exist. Underneath the dark grey line -- the dark black line there is a light grey line, and the light grey line shows the same pattern with the statistical effect of the NATO and KLA activity removed from the original line. Okay. We have extracted the statistical relationship of the KLA and NATO on total killings, and we have then re-shown, re-plotted total killings. Okay. The statistical term for this is the residual. The underlying light grey line is the residual, that which remains after the effect of NATO and KLA activity has been removed. The point of -- the interpretation of these graphs and the point that I think is so useful from these is that it allows us simultaneously to consider both the effect of NATO and the KLA all at the same time over the entire period, not on a single day, not on a single peak, but over the entire period. And what we see is that removing the effect of NATO and the KLA has no substantive impact on the patterns that we see, and that's the fundamental conclusion. So again, returning to figure 20 for the north region, the upper left graph, we see that the light grey line tracks the dark black line in every substantive particular. It rises during the early phase, the first phase, drops dramatically on the night of the 6/7 April cease-fire, stays at a low point, and then rises again. You can see that it is a very close transition. There are throughout these eight graphs a few anomalies. Some of them are discussed in the text. Some of them, I would be happy to discuss at more length now, if you prefer, but these two graphs in particular are the heart of our argument that we should reject the claim that either NATO or the KLA are plausible causes of killing and migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Therefore, the essence or the gist of your analysis is precisely this part and the conclusion that the KLA did not have any impact on migration. You probably are unfamiliar with some testimony by Albanians before this Chamber inter alia the chief of the general -- the main staff of the KLA, who stated something to the contrary. He stated that the KLA ordered civilians to withdraw alongside troops. Had you had those testimonies before you and had you been able to see what was the extent of the KLA's orders for civilians to move together with them, would that have had any impact on the results of your findings?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's refer to figure 21. First off, I would have -- I would make it a practice to ignore any claim by a politician about what people do or don't do in response to his orders. But I'm interested in the patterns, I'm interested in what people actually did rather than what people were told to do --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may interrupt. We had witnesses which obeyed such orders. In combination with everything aforementioned, would that have had an impact on your standpoint?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there were some people who did obey those orders. The question is: Did the hundreds and hundreds of thousands of people obey those orders or some other pattern? That's my question. That's what is interesting me and what is the core of this report. No doubt, one can find someone who will say they followed such and such an order, but if we observe the graphs on figure 21, it seems to me that where we look at refugee flow we see that removing the effect of the KLA and NATO does not leave as clean a line as figure 20, and we discussed this at some length in the text, but nonetheless, in the substantive conclusions, particularly for the major peaks in each of the regions where we make findings, the patterns are similar. To review, our argument is that in the south and west there is a major peak in the early period which declines dramatically at the 6/7 April point, whereas in the north and east the major peak comes in the middle period between the 7th and 24th of April. Here we find that the residual patterns track closely the original lines. There is an exception in the east which is dominated by Pristina, and we have some discussion of that in the text. That is the place where there seems to be some question about this relationship, but the other seven graphs are all -- all four killing graphs and the other three migration graphs are extremely close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you as part of that answer refer to the middle period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The middle period is of interest to us particularly in the north and east where we see more action in the middle period in both -- in both figures 20 and 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which you described as the 27th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 6th to the 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 6th to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 24th, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. The transcript hasn't picked this up, but that clarifies it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. All of the graphs have a pattern of dark banding and then light banding, and the intention of those bands is to distinguish the three phases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow that. It's just I'm trying to get your answer expressed clearly in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We as attorneys at law love to talk, but I think you far exceed us. All I wanted to hear from you was this. The data you received was from your interviews with people. Had you had data derived from such interviews about these issues, would that have had any impact on your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of our data is from interviews but not all of it. Some of our data is from exhumation records, other data is from administrative records. It's not all interview data, so that's an important clarification. I'm not sure what issues you're referring to that would have changed it. I've already answered your question that I'm not interested in people's personal attribution about why they did something or am I interested in a given politician's claim that he has such and such influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the reason why people fled. I suppose that you weren't able to establish that based on exhumation data. We're talking about the data you collected at the border post or the border crossing. Had you had such data at the time, would that have had any impact on the findings of your report, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the border post we asked people only where they came from, when they left, when they crossed the border. We did not ask them why they crossed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That explains it all. I received this document from my learned friend Mr. Fila. He says he discussed it with our learned friend Mr. Stamp, who did not object to showing this document to Dr. Ball.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With Court's permission, if you find that necessary, we can do that in order to clarify whether there were any interruptions between the 6th of April -- on the 6th of April concerning migration flow of refugees. If you deem it inappropriate, we will certainly accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's impossible to tell because we don't know what your document says, but since there's no objection, perhaps you could have it displayed on the ELMO and ask whatever question you wish to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wasn't the one who spoke to Mr. Stamp, so I personally am not acquainted with his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the total of the document is that the witness is being shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I thought counsel would explain what the document is that the witness is being shown. But have a look at the document. We have no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's have it on the ELMO and ask whatever question you wish to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On my document something is written by one of our clients and if possible if Mr. Stamp can provide a document which is a clean version of the same. If the usher can take it from Mr. Stamp. If we can go just bit down so it's -- now it can be seen the source. It says "UNHCR Geneva October the 15th, 1999."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, Dr. Ball, you can see on this document that there is no interruption of the refugee flow from the 6th of April onwards until the 10th, as you claimed. So did you have this document in front of you before you composed your report or this is the first time you see it and how you can comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually this is -- we've already discussed this document, counsel. I discussed it in direct, and I consider -- and I discussed why I consider it to be unreliable. It is graphed along with the other sources in figure 3 of my 28 January 2007 report, people leaving Kosovo, four sources. And I've already discussed that I consider it unreliable because it shows a batching effect whereby numbers are averaged or totals are averaged across and you see curiously flat lines, weird plateaus through the data that shows that data was batched up and reported by Geneva at specific points rather than when the data occurred. I can repeat my critique if that's useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I remember your answer. So you still maintain your position that this document is unreliable and you do not accept it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is unreliable because it was collected in Geneva. It was too far from the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Dr. Ball. That's all the questions I have had for you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since the document doesn't exist in any other form, I think it should be given an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC122, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I just indicate to the Court the document is substantially a reproduction of page 1. It's a reproduction of a page in Exhibit P737 which is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have it in its current form and I would like actually to see it again, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just doing it just so that later on there could be ease of cross-reference. It is substantially a reduction of page 1 of Exhibit P737.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour, for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, have we exhausted you? Further cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Ball, Judge Bonomy has invited some discussion with you about what we may have learned from consultation with other experts in this field. I think I'll accept that invitation just very briefly. I mentioned the name yesterday of a statistician from I believe the University of Wisconsin by the name of John Steele. I want to read you something and just get your comment on it if I can. Commenting on your reports, your testimony, in Milosevic. "There are two levels to address reliability. First, is the analysis technically correct and secondly, how reliable is the inference of the causal relationship based on the analysis. The problem I see here is that there is little or no precedent with regard to how reliably one can make the inference in this and similar cases. It's not been done often enough in cases where the cause is, in fact, known. The whole concept suffers from a lack of ground truth, as it were. Perhaps the expert can address that issue, but I suspect not. What he has done really seems to be called heuristic statistics, seeking to understand something or to generate testable hypotheses by a data analysis. Such studies can be very useful, but they are not themselves conclusive. They can point the way for more studies, but do not themselves confirm by hypotheses coming from them." What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an impressively careful statement. I do not agree with the statement "heuristic statistic," but I do agree that more studies would be helpful. Let me go back, though, point by point, because it's actually -- there's terms of art in nearly every line. "Is there little or no precedent with regard to how reliably one can make the inference in this and similar cases?" In human rights, certainly not; however, the methods in historical demography with respect to migration and the methods and the adjustment of censuses with respect to multiple systems estimation are fairly well-known, in fact, we have hundreds of references that we could provide. We've provided several dozen in the original report. It's easy enough to generate many, many more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do you identify human rights and what is it about human rights that makes it any different from carrying out the analysis in any other field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be crass about it, Your Honour, money. Nobody cares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People care a lot about censuses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't mean to ask you why perhaps it hadn't been done. What is it about the field of human rights that makes it any different in the sense of making the work that you do any different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe it does, Your Honour, which is why I've applied the methods in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, I have to question the description of the field that you're actually in as the human rights field, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- there's little point in us debating that here so please carry on with your analysis of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it possible to scroll back the transcript so that I can see the question because it was a very, very precise statement or put it on the other screen. It was an enormously carefully crafted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you can now see it, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- oh, here we go, yes. Now I can. It's very fuzzy. A little bit higher. Can we scroll up another half-dozen lines. There we go. Stop. Thank you. Thank you. That's very helpful. The claim that Professor Steele is making is that we have used the statistics to generate the testable hypotheses, and to the contrary, we drew the hypotheses from the political debate swirling about the conflict in Kosovo. So we certainly did not use this sort of -- this sense of heuristic statistics where we generated the hypotheses from the data analysis. We generated the hypotheses from the -- from the political debate and tried to quantify those hypotheses in ways that would be testable. Similarly, I noticed that Professor Steele talks about the confirmation of hypotheses. Again, he's quite right. The confirmation of hypotheses would depend on a case-control study, not an observational one. This is purely an observational study and so we have confined ourselves very strictly to the disconfirmation of hypotheses, which is, in fact, a much simpler intellectual exercise. It is much easier to reject hypotheses which are clearly contradicted by data than it is to confirm hypotheses which requires a much more elaborate experimental design, which in that -- oops. The screen just went blank. But confirming hypothesis requires a fairly elaborate experimental design and is far beyond the capacity of a statistician to conduct in this kind of -- in a real political situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try one more, and to some extent, I think you have already answered this at least a little bit today. So understand that you won't need to repeat things you've already commented on. Here's the statement: "The causal reasoning in the expert's report and testimony has a possibly significant flaw. He is relying on temporal relationships and making the assumption that a cause must precede its effect, thus he rules out, say, NATO strikes as being causal of refugee flow because they took place after the flow began. However, it may be that one cannot apply this kind of logic to human beings, since we are somewhat capable of anticipating future events. In that situation, the usual causal logic may not be applicable. If you see rain clouds gathering overhead and move your party indoors, is the cause the clouds or the anticipated rain storm? How can one really assign causation in such a situation? Can one really say that the rain did not cause you to move indoors?"

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That strikes me as interesting psychological speculation, but I'm willing to stand on several hundred years' of western logic in which we assume cause to precede effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess that's what you'd say but, you know, I think the point there is that if you go indoors because you see rain clouds, then the cause of your going indoors may be to avoid rain, but it doesn't rain until sometime after you've gone indoors, and that's the problem I guess Dr. Steele and I both see in your analysis, saying that the bombing preceded the movement in a situation where it was pretty well clear to everyone in Albania, I think, that there was the imminence of NATO bombing was there and -- something one had to get away from. I think that's the point that Dr. Steele was trying to make and the one that I have been trying to make. Maybe that was more of a comment than a question, but if you have something to say about it go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think this is an like an excellent -- I mean, I am greatly hopeful that this is near the close. It seems like an excellent place to come full circle to the first major figure in the original January 2002 report because that addresses precisely the point you're raising. If it were the case that people were to leave their homes because they believed that they were going to be bombed in your rain cloud analogy, that might at some level be plausible. But how did they get killed? As we show in figure after figure, figures starting with figure 2 in our original -- I'm sorry, I'm not sure which figure it is. You guys had me moving back and forth and it will take a while for me to find the figures. But in the original report, when we show the correlation between killings and migration, the killings match the migration perfectly. Now, I'm willing to agree that we might move a picnic indoors if we see rain clouds because we anticipate the cause of the rain. I'm unwilling to believe that we will then massacre everyone at the picnic in anticipation of the rain. And what we find here, sir, is that the killings and migration match each other over and over again. They match each other at the global level, at the top level across Kosovo. They match each other at the regional level. They match each other at the municipal level. While your claims about people's anticipation might make sense for bombing, they make no sense whatsoever with respect to killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we might be able to get into some issues of coincidence here but I don't think I want to do that. I think we're close enough to the end that maybe I can go into one more issue with you, and it's one that certainly troubles me. I don't know whether it troubles anyone else. And that is that you only used data from this one border point, the Morina border point. And in Milosevic at page 2157 when you were asked about this you said: "That one border point was sufficient because, according to the available data, I believe that more than half of all Kosovar Albanians who left Kosovo did so through this point." So when you say "I believe that more than half left through this point," are we saying that that's simply some belief you have or is that based on some kind of hard data that you had available that would prove that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're so troubled, Mr. Ackerman. You've used that term many times. You must not sleep well. Perhaps I can help. If you examine the appendices to the Policy or Panic report you'll find an elaborate sensitivity analysis in which we compare refugee flow to a number of countries, principally Macedonia in addition to Albania, but other crossing points in Albania as well as Bosnia, and we do not have extensive and detailed information about the people in Macedonia or in Bosnia or from the other crossing points in Albania. Macedonia, Bosnia, or other crossing points in Albania. But we have some information about them and we used that information to, again, create simulations to say how different would those people's patterns have to have been in order to change our results based principally on the data from the Morina border point. And we found that we would have to make radical assumptions about the people entering Macedonia and Bosnia, that they would have to be completely different in their points of origin and in their patterns of movement. And we found that unlikely given the limited survey data we have from both places, which indicate that people were behaving in roughly very similar ways to the people entering Albania. So it was not a belief based on some sort of instinct but rather on a fairly detailed sensitivity analysis which is available to you should you choose to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, in Milosevic you went on to say this about that: "All the other evidence available from other border points in Albania as well as the border points in Macedonia and data from Bosnia suggest," emphasise 'suggest,' "that their movement patterns and departure patterns were substantially similar," emphasis 'substantially similar,' "to the patterns found among refugees who entered Albania." Now, first of all, the terms "suggest" and "substantially similar" are not terms of art in your field, are they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Both of them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used "suggest" because we do not say "prove" nor do we say "confirm." We say "suggest" because this is the kind of evidence which alone would leave us speculating, but we would present in a process of fact-finding so that it can contribute with other forms of evidence to make a broader conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, did you actually receive data from these other border points that you talk about here that was like the data that you received at Morina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the data from those other border points was compiled? Was it someone using clickers or did you have data that showed when people left their homes and where they came from?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had -- no, we did not have evidence from the border points about when people left their -- where -- excuse me -- where people came from. We had evidence on the gross numbers of people crossing rather crudely aggregated across time that was available from UNHCR. We then conducted surveys -- well, I had a group of colleagues that -- "we" is in a very broad sense here. I had a group of colleagues from the University of California Berkeley who conducted almost 2.000 surveys among refugees in Bosnia and -- from the Human Rights Centre at Berkeley, and we used the surveys conducted by Physicians for Human Rights were conducted -- which were conducted on a probability basis in refugees camps in Macedonia. It was on the basis of those two surveys that we concluded that people's movement patterns were substantially the same as the people in -- as the refugees in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Since you told us that the word "suggest," for instance, is a term of art, then can you tell us with regard to this data a percentage probability figure that is accurate, that it suggests it but to what level of accuracy? Are you at 95 per cent? Are you at 70 per cent? Where are you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's not a probability associated with it; instead, it is analysed via a sensitivity analysis. I don't have that in front of me. If we could pull it up, I'd be happy to walk you through it. It's in the appendix of "Policy or Panic" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've answered my question. I really don't want to go through your sensitivity now. So you --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hang on. That --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. May I finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to hear the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you derive a probability? Is there a way you can do it? I know you didn't do it, but is there a way you can?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not a way to derive a probability in a formal sense. There is, however, a way to - which is what we did - derive the range of plausible outcomes based on a wide variation in assumptions about things that may have biased the underlying surveys. There is not a strict probability measure for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. You went on then again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are going to refer, then, to the appendix to "Policy or Panic" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE BONOMY -- to do what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were going to do that for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To show how the sensitivity analysis had been conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you need to do that specifically or to direct our attention to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would direct your attention to it. If there are questions about the validity of our broader analysis, I would be happy to clarify them at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You went on in Milosevic at page 2310 on this same subject: "I examined survey information from other places and considered what the likely pattern from those places would be," the likely pattern. Now, that means you don't have enough data to construct a pattern; you just consider a likely pattern and guessed at what the likely pattern might be?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ackerman, as I suspect you know. What a likely pattern is is a pattern that you look at from sample data. When you have sample data, you do not know what the necessary pattern is. You don't know, because you only have a little bit of the data. So what you do with the sample is you make an estimate of what the pattern would be and that estimate is subject to the error that -- or the margin of error that governs the sampling process. So I hope that is sufficient, but it is not a -- it's not a guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You went on --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This carried on in Milosevic with some more --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- answers. And you say this: "We know something," talking about what went on at these other border points, "we know something from the counts kept by the Albanian border guards at two other primary crossing points. We know something -- although, in my opinion, with quite a bit of error, we know something about refugees who crossed into Macedonia, and we do know something about refugees who crossed into Bosnia, and we know a little bit with less certainty about those who crossed into Montenegro."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what you then finally say in Milosevic that you can -- you think you can take it from assumption to reasonable estimate.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That's your term. What I mean by something is again an attempt to explain to lay people the difference between the quality of our scientific understanding of the cross -- of the people who crossed at Morina relative to the people who crossed at other places. We know something. We have a considerable error around that. Knowing something with error is not an assumption, sir, and I'm afraid to have to have repeated this. I kept -- started keeping track of these corrections this morning. This is now the seventh time I've corrected you on this point. I hope that we can become clearer as we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I wasn't using my words. I was using yours words.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You are introducing the term "assumption" repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here are your exact words: "So knowing those other things, I think we can narrow the claim I've made from an assumption to, I think, a reasonable estimate." Now, those are your words. I didn't make up that word "assumption." You used it in Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: By refuting it, Mr. Ackerman, by saying that we have made an estimate. Okay. Finding the word in a sentence is not the same as me asserting it, as you with I believe your elaborate training in logic, should understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well -- okay. I thought I was through, but I've got to do one more thing, if I can find it. At page 56, line 9, when Mr. Lukic was asking you questions about people leaving before there was ever any bombing, first you said this: "If there were convoys before the bombing, clearly, the bombing did not cause those convoys of refugees to be on the move." And then very shortly after that you said: "I have no idea why they're moving." So wouldn't it be fair to say that what you said in that first statement, that "clearly, the bombing did not cause those convoys of refugees to be on the move" was just an assumption on your part?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it was not. I don't know why they were moving, but I think I can be clear why they were not moving. I know what their -- the reason was not; that does not mean that I know what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you said these people are certainly not moving because their region is being bombed which is different from what you said in your first statement with regard to it. Now, if you have more to say it --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, this strikes me as sophistry. I'm not sure that I can clarify further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you have more to say about that you can, but otherwise I'm finished with my questions and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The recent exchanges are matters that we can reflect upon at the end of our -- when we come to deliberate; they're not matters that need any further explanation from you, Dr. Ball. I have at this stage two questions. One is for Mr. Stamp. There's been some reference in the recent questions to this border crossing point at Morina and on the second occasion that Mr. -- that Dr. Ball gave evidence in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic, he was presented with a number of documents to try to identify the locus. Now, are they exhibits in this case because they don't appear on your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we all satisfied that we know where this crossing point was and that the issue that appeared to be such a big one for Milosevic is no longer an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I thought so that it was clarified clearly in Milosevic where he marked a map on the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, he?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He marked a map in Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I can produce it but it wasn't raised. I thought that was a settled issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If we haven't seen the map, we don't know where it is. Please don't keep secrets from us, Mr. Stamp. If you want to prove the case you may have to produce that material so that we can be satisfied. You're right that it hasn't been challenged in the cross-examination, but I still think that you should produce the material that was used to establish the crossing point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other question is one I have for you, Dr. Ball, that may display a basic misunderstanding of something but I hope it doesn't. Mr. Milosevic tried to ask you about the notion that NATO and the KLA were working together and tried to suggest that that was a separate hypothesis from the three that you were working on. First of all, is that a different hypothesis from any of the three you were working on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be a separate hypothesis in order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And second -- well, I think that answers that question. My second question then is have you somehow or other in the 2007 report dealt with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the reason is the same that I explained to Milosevic, that in order for a combined or interaction effect to have -- to have meaning in a statistical analysis, both of the underlining components must themselves have been significant. They both themselves must have had values that were significantly different from zero by -- they could not have occurred by chance. That did not occur in any of the four models until consequently we were unable to calculate any meaningful test of an interaction between the two. I think I may have said it in less formal language then, but that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You seem to have been prevented from dealing with the question in that trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I don't think I have understood your answer at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me a little. Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by both of the underlying events must themselves have been significant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And they both must have had values that was significantly different from zero.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. So when we construct a statistical model, the logic is that we are predicting some value, we are trying to make an estimate of something. In the case of the analyses that we got to this morning with the estimate of the total number of killings and migration, we're estimating the total numbers of killings and migration and we're using information -- even though we know those values, we're using information about KLA and NATO activities to try and make those predictions. Okay. So the idea is to determine how good a prediction of killings and migration we can make based on our knowledge of NATO and KLA activity. The core test about whether or not we have managed to make a reasonable -- whether or not one of the effects, in this case KLA or NATO activity, whether that effect has some impact is whether we can look at the value that we calculate for the level of its impact and distinguish that value from zero. And the reason we do that is because in any statistical model some values will occur by chance and we have to be able to rule out that the value we have discovered has occurred by chance. If we fail to find the values of, in this case, the KLA actions and the NATO actions, both as significantly different from zero, that we can reject the claim that these both could have occurred by chance, then we can construct a combined measure of the two and test whether the combined measure of an interaction between the KLA and NATO, which would test the idea that they were working together, could itself be a further higher-order cause of killing and migration -- killing and/or migration. However, in none of the four models we examined were we able to find both KLA and NATO effects that were significantly different from zero. So it's as if we had to multiple two numbers, one of which could have been zero, and so that would have been a meaningless exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm still struggling, I'm afraid. You've been able, obviously in relation to each of them, separately, to come to the conclusion that their effects were significantly different from zero, otherwise you would never have been able to deal with the hypothesis in relation to each of these two separately or have I misunderstood something totally here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some models we had some values that were significantly different from zero, in others not. In fact, the strictest possible rejection of the claim that NATO, for example, was the cause of the killings, would be to find that its effect could have occurred by chance. That would be a sort of slam-dunk rejection of the NATO hypothesis. However, we found that in some of our models NATO had a significant effect and in some of the models KLA had a significant effect but not in the same model. Okay. So it was not that we could pick a model and then test the interaction of the two. That's the limitation, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, are you saying the job couldn't be done on the material that you had, or that that actually does demonstrate something negative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could not be done given the material. I would hesitate to speculate further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Do you have re-examination, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know how long, roughly, you'll be?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me check with the interpretation because of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, before we do, it might well be wise to take the adjournment here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the reason I don't want to do that is because it takes time to make arrangements for the next witness, and therefore I'm anxious that these arrangements should be made during the break and not cause us to be interrupted again later in the day. So I'd like to find out if the interpreters could bear with us until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Until 1.00, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you can --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Continue to 1.00. If we don't make it, we don't make it, but let's see if we can make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I wanted to do was to find Exhibits 70 and 71 in the Milosevic case which I referred to at pages 2320 of the transcript in which the witness clarified where Morina was. There were two Morinas; one on the Albanian side of the border where he and his team collected material and there was another Morina somewhere within Kosovo which I had thought settled that issue. But I would think that I should bring the map because I have a copy of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary. I think you can produce that as an exhibit and we can interpret the evidence in the light of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary to go back over it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe I could just ask him one question to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You recall in the Milosevic case you were shown a map of southern Kosovo and you identified the village of Morina near to which was a border crossing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this village of Morina on the Kosovo side or the Albanian side of the border?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Albanian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, about how far from the border was this village?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few dozen metres. It's just a scattered bunch of houses and a border post. There's not much there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. You said in cross-examination that you received United States government support for your work, including the principal report, that is, support from the United States State Department and United States AID. Can you just tell us briefly the nature of the support and whether or not the support had any role in your statistical work.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The money was given to our partners at the ABA/CEELI they subgranted that money to us at the American Association for the Advancement of Science. I had no reporting relationship with CEELI on that money other than to conduct the research and I had no relationship whatsoever with the State Department. I made one presentation to the State Department. They asked no questions of any substantive nature, nor did they offer any suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you explained this quite adequately, but since you were asked a couple of times in different forms, the system that you used to determine the time at which people left their homes during the period when there was a report of this unilateral cease-fire by the Yugoslav government. Now, was the system used to measure the time the people left their home based on a calculation for a model or was it based on the actual report of the people from the individual interviews, or maybe I should ask you just to explain how you worked out the period when they left their home.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The short answer is that both are true. Models are built from data, so we built the model of transit time from the information given to us in a series of interviews that we collected and that -- that Human Rights Watch collected and that Physicians For Human Rights collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were -- it was read to you a passage from your article entitled "Statistics and Slobodan," in which it was stated - and I am paraphrasing now, because I don't have the exact quotation right here - that it was not possible in which -- the assertion was made in which you said it was not possible to separate the actions of the KLA and Yugoslav forces. Do you recall that or would you like me to find it? And I think you wanted to explain the context in which you made that statement in that article. Would you like to look at the article before you answer or can you --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's unnecessary. The context was that given the data we had, it was not possible to separate those actions. It would be possible if one had extensive evidence on the movements of Yugoslav forces. That would be a quite different study and could be done, but we didn't have that data.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. An issue was raised as to whether or not it was valid or accurate for you to be estimating exactly 10.356 people killed, and I think you were trying to explain that it was an estimate and that there was a margin or a confidence interval. Can you look at page 6 of your report, the principal report, the second paragraph beginning "second."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the third line from the bottom, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You gave there the confidence interval.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And prior to that, you said that the estimate was generated by means of a widely used demographic statistical technique known as multiple systems estimation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you -- I know it's elaborated upon in your appendix, but can you in two sentences in layman's terms explain how does a multiple systems estimation work, especially in light of the fact that you have had recent figures in respect to death -- deaths which confirm the older figures that you used.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BALL [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I think the new data confirmed the pattern of the data that we presented earlier. We have no -- we've neither confirmed nor disconfirmed the total estimate using the new data. As I explained before, that would require substantially greater resources. Multiple systems estimation, there are a couple of metaphors which might be possible, but I think that the easiest to understand is to imagine that we approach a dark room and we have a handful of small rubber balls that bounce very vigorously. And the idea that we have is that we would like to have some sense of how big the room is. We can't go in and measure it for some reason, but we throw the balls into the room as hard as we can and we listen to the balls bouncing about, and we can hear the balls striking each other on occasion and we hear the balls click, click, striking each other. We then gather the balls, go to another room, and throw the balls again with the same force into the second room and we again listen for the balls to spread through the room and then occasionally hit each other, and we hear them striking click, click, click, click, click. We would draw the inference that the second room is considerably smaller than the first room, because using the same number of balls and the same number of force to throw into the room, the balls encounter each other more frequently because there's less room for them to spread into the space. Similarly multiple systems estimation is a process of taking the enumerations of some kind of phenomenon, in this case human deaths, human killings, and saying that each of the projects, the seven projects we now have that have enumerated deaths have in some sense been thrown into the space of deaths that occurred in Kosovo during this period. And what we then do is measure how often these projects encounter each other, how often do they bump into each other in that space. The more frequently they bump into each other, then the smaller the space we infer to be. The less frequently they bump into each other, the more they spread out in that space, the larger we infer that space to be. Another approach, another intuitive approach to the same problem is the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we understand this well enough not to have such a long answer, Dr. Ball. I thought I understood it before the question was asked, and I don't think it really justifies this extensive further investigation. Please carry on with something else, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor.
